---
title: "Models and Evaluation"
subtitle: "How predictable is shortage onset, and which choices matter?"
---

This page summarizes the Milestone 3 modeling. The full analysis, with code, tuning details,
feature ablation, calibration, subgroup results, and error analysis, is on the
[Modeling Notebook](modeling.ipynb) page.

## Modeling question

Using only what is known at the end of year *t*−1, how well can drugs be ranked by their risk of a
new shortage onset in year t? This is RQ1, and the same models are then used to answer the
other three [research questions](questions.qmd):

| Research question | What is modeled |
|---|---|
| RQ1: How predictable is onset? | Each at-risk drug's risk of a new shortage next year, used as a ranking (a watchlist) |
| RQ2: What distinguishes drugs that go short? | Logistic-regression odds ratios, and performance as feature groups are added |
| RQ3: Do manufacturers exit first? | Whether exit features add predictive value beyond the others (a predictive test, not yet the planned event study) |
| RQ4: Does it hold across drug types? | The same predictions scored within injectable and oral drugs, and transfer from one group to the other |

**Data:** One row per drug (ingredient per route) per year, 2020–2025, restricted to drugs on the
market and not already in shortage on January 1: about 11,500 at-risk drug-years with only 161
onsets (about 1.8%). Predicting that a running shortage continues is easy and useless, so those
rows are excluded.

**Features:** (13, all measured as of December 31 of *t*−1): route group, years since first
approval, an approved-before-1982 flag, packages, approvals, and manufacturers on the market, a
prior-shortage flag, prior-year recalls, and four prior-year exit measures. Anything known only
once a shortage exists (FDA's stated reason, days since posting) is banned as source of leakage.

## Methods and rationale

| Model | Role | Why it is here |
|---|---|---|
| **Prior shortage** | Baseline | Promised in the research questions: flag drugs with an earlier shortage |
| **Route rate** | Baseline | Each drug gets its route group's training-year onset rate; route is the largest single difference found in exploration |
| **Logistic regression** (L2) | Candidate | Few parameters, stable with about 100 positives, and its coefficients answer RQ2 directly. Counts are log-transformed because they are heavily skewed. |
| **Random forest** | Candidate | Finds thresholds and interactions (e.g. age mattering more for injectables) without hand-built terms; indifferent to skew |
| **Gradient-boosted trees** | Candidate | The same strengths as the forest, fit sequentially; tested because it is often the strongest tabular learner |


## Evaluation design

{{< embed modeling.ipynb#fig-validation-design >}}

- **Rolling-origin validation:** Each test year (2021,2022, 2023) is
  predicted by a model trained on all earlier years. Random  k-fold would train on 2023 to predict
  2021, leaking the later base rate and the later meaning of shortage history.
- **Nested tuning: ** Hyperparameters are chosen by the same rolling scheme inside the training
  years only. The 2021 fold has one training year, so it uses defaults fixed in advance.
- **Pooled scoring:** The three test years are pooled into 5,700 drug-years with 103 onsets.
  2024–2025 (14 onsets, after the rate of  new shortages collapsed) are a separate robustness check, not used
  for model selection.
- **Metrics:** PR-AUC compared with the 1.8% base rate is primary, because at this base rate
  ROC-AUC can look respectable while the top of the list is mostly false alarms. ROC-AUC, onsets
  caught by a 50-drug watchlist each year, and calibration (Brier skill score, reliability plot)
  are reported alongside. Accuracy and F1 are not reported: at a 0.5 threshold every model
  predicts "no," and doing nothing scores 98% accuracy.
- **Uncertainty: ** 95% intervals come from 1,000 bootstrap resamples of whole drugs (the same
  drug appears in several years), and model differences are paired on the same resamples.

## Key results

{{< embed modeling.ipynb#fig-model-comparison >}}

| Model | PR-AUC (95% interval) | × base rate | ROC-AUC (95% interval) | PR-AUC vs logistic regression | Onsets in top 50 (of 103) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Prior shortage (baseline) | 0.024 (0.018–0.034) | 1.4 | 0.55 (0.52–0.59) | −0.017 (−0.033 to −0.008) | 5 |
| Route rate (baseline) | 0.031 (0.023–0.040) | 1.7 | 0.66 (0.61–0.71) | −0.011 (−0.026 to −0.003) | 5 |
| **Logistic regression** | **0.041 (0.031–0.060)** | **2.3** | **0.72 (0.67–0.76)** | — | 6 |
| Random forest | 0.037 (0.028–0.053) | 2.1 | 0.70 (0.65–0.75) | −0.004 (−0.016 to +0.006) | 10 |
| Gradient boosting | 0.032 (0.025–0.043) | 1.8 | 0.68 (0.63–0.73) | −0.009 (−0.022 to −0.001) | 7 |

: Pooled test years 2021–2023 (5,700 drug-years, 103 onsets, base rate 1.81%). A random 50-drug
watchlist would catch about 3 onsets over the three years. {#tbl-comparison}

- Onsets are modestly predictable: Every candidate beats both baselines. Logistic regression
  is best on both summary metrics (PR-AUC 2.3× the base rate, ROC-AUC 0.72), and its riskiest 20%
  of drugs each year contain about half of the onsets (52 of 103).
- The candidates can't be separated reliably: Logistic regression's lead over the random
  forest has an interval spanning 0, and the best model changes from year to year. Its lead over
  gradient boosting is small but excludes 0.
- Precision at the top is low for everyone: a 50-drug watchlist is right 4% to 7% of the time.
- Selected model: L2 logistic regression (`C` = 0.3 once tuning had data). It ties or beats
  the trees on every ranking metric, has better-calibrated probabilities, is the simplest to
  reproduce, and is interpretable.

 So, where is the signal? Adding feature groups one at a time shows that route, drug
age, and the pre-1982 flag alone reach the full model's performance (PR-AUC 0.042, ROC-AUC 0.72).
Market size, history and quality, and exits each change PR-AUC by at most 0.002, with every
interval spanning 0.

{{< embed modeling.ipynb#fig-coefficients >}}

**Robustness checks.**

- Calibration: In 2021–2023 probabilities are roughly right but a little high (2.3% predicted
  vs 1.8% observed), and the Brier skill score is barely above 0 (0.007): the value is in the
  ranking. After 2023 the ranking held (ROC-AUC 0.82 in 2024, on 11 onsets) but every model
  predicted about 2% risk when the real rate fell to 0.56% (2024) and 0.15% (2025).
- Injectable vs oral: Within each group ranking is weaker (ROC-AUC 0.61 for injectables, 0.66
  for oral drugs, intervals overlapping), and a model trained on one group ranks the other about
  as well as a model trained on it.

## Interpretation

- **RQ1-** Shortage onset is predictable a year ahead, but only modestly, and mostly from route
  and drug age. A ranked watchlist concentrates risk; it does not pinpoint which drugs will go short.
- **RQ2-.** Holding the other features fixed, injectables have about 3.4 times the odds of oral
  drugs, each 10 years since first approval raises the odds about 43%, and a prior shortage about
  65%. Market size and number of manufacturers show no clear effect once route and age are known.
  These are associations: route and age mark a kind of market (old, low-margin sterile
  manufacturing), not causes.
- **RQ3-** Year-level exits in NSDE add no predictive value. That is not evidence that exits
  don't matter: NSDE exit dates lag and are often administrative, and an effect confined to small
  markets wouldn't move pooled metrics. The planned event study is still needed.
- **RQ4-** Predictability is similarly modest for injectable and oral drugs, and the pattern
  transfers between them.
- **Misses and Failure Modes ** False alarms are the textbook shortage profile, old generic
  injectables that usually don't go short in a given year (though 9.7% of them did in a later year,
  against 2.1% of other drugs). Missed onsets are newer, often brand-name oral drugs hit by acute
  shocks such as the ADHD stimulant demand surge or impurity recalls, which these supply-side
  features can't see.

Possible next steps: The RQ3 event study focused on small markets, resetting probabilities to a
current base rate, and demand-side features (Medicare spending, if it can be linked) for the
acute shortages the model misses. Demand side features would be our preferred next avenue of investigation.
